item.title: How Spiritual Maturity Is Linked to a Healthier Mind
item.description:
Growing faith doesn’t have to be just a spiritual journey. It can also be a journey toward good mental health. The deep connection between a spiritual relationship with God and a stable, grounded mind provides a profound basis for spiritual maturity.

“Bible Study”, Courtesy of Daiga Ellaby, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License; This develops through years of navigating difficulty, learning to trust what cannot always be seen, and holding onto faith even when it seems distant. Along the way, there is a growth that quietly reshapes how a person thinks and processes emotion.

Some of the outward markers of a mature faith are familiar: deeper compassion, a longer view on hardship, and greater patience. However, the internal work to cultivate these qualities does something else. It builds a resilient, settled mind that can sustain genuine peace. This kind of growth comes with a promise that speaks directly to the peace available to those who trust in God.

The steadfast of mind You will keep in perfect peace, because he trusts in You. – Isaiah 26:3, NASB

Steadfast means fixed and anchored. These are qualities that describe other areas of mature faith. A mind that is anchored in the trust of God’s promise discovers that peace is no longer a destination. It becomes a natural outcome of having a deeper relationship with God.

The Link Between Spiritual Maturity and Mental Health

Health professionals are becoming more aware of the connection between spiritual well-being and mental wellness. An individual whose faith has been tested repeatedly tends to develop an inner stability not found elsewhere.

These individuals have cultivated a mature faith throughout the years, and they often report lower levels of anxiety and a greater ability to move through grief with greater strength. These are not accidental outcomes. They are the natural product of a life shaped by ongoing surrender and honest reflection about placing trust in something larger than oneself.

This is not to say that spiritually grounded people are immune to mental health challenges. Life is hard, and with it come tough moments, regardless of how deep one’s faith may run. It is the framework developed through years of spiritual investment that can significantly reduce the emotional weight a person carries.

The way a person can make meaning of a difficulty or find footing when the ground shifts is a pattern that Christian counselors often observe in those with a well-developed faith. This becomes the stabilizing force during seasons of uncertainty and significant life transitions. The pain is not erased, but the way it is held is changed.

For God has not given us a spirit of timidity, but of power and love and discipline. – 2 Timothy 1:7, NASB

This verse reflects a spiritual discipline that is intentional and practiced, deepening faith over time. The focus shifts from emotional reactivity to grounded, purposeful engagement with life. It is an engagement that is built through consistent spiritual investment rather than a single pivotal moment.

What a Rooted Faith Does for the Mind

When faith has grown roots through regular prayer, community, ongoing study, and the experience accumulated in a life of walking with God through hard seasons, it changes how a person relates to their thoughts and emotions. They are no longer swept away by worry or fear. They have learned to pause and return to what is known to be true. This practice builds strength to resist the pull toward catastrophic thinking.

This does not mean individuals should suppress difficult emotions or pretend that painful things are not painful. It compels them to create a consistent place to bring these emotions, where they can be managed without collapsing under them.

Emotional regulation is one of the strongest predictors of long-term mental health and resilience. A faith that is rooted, combined with consistent prayer and connection to an authentic community of believers, reduces the likelihood of processing hard seasons in isolation. Isolation is one of the most significant risk factors for declining mental health.

The presence of both spiritual and relational resources creates a life that is held in multiple ways and a mind that learns, over time, that it does not have to carry every burden alone. Scripture describes a practice that is active and ongoing rather than a single act of faith.

It does require a rhythm developed over time to gradually reshape how the mind processes stress, fear, and uncertainty. Scripture invites a person to meet anxiety with prayer and gratitude when making requests known to God.

Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and pleading with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. – Philippians 4:6, NASB

Spiritual Maturity and the Practice of Peace

One of the most rewarding mental health benefits of spiritual maturity is the deepened capacity for peace. This is not the absence of problems, but a settled mindset that persists as a person experiences them.

Those who have been walking in faith for years describe a meaningful shift in how they approach difficult situations. The overwhelming feelings they once carried have gradually been met with steadiness. This shift comes from a growing trust that something larger and more purposeful is at work, even in the hardest and most disorienting seasons of life.

When it comes to mental well-being, this internal shift carries significant weight. Persistent anxiety and chronic stress are two common concerns that Christian counselors encounter in daily work with clients. Spiritual maturity offers a perspective on these experiences that goes beyond immediate circumstances and frames the present difficulty within the context of a God-authored story.

The result of this reframing is a healing potential that situates hard things within a narrative that includes hope, purpose, and forward movement. When this perspective deepens as the person continues to walk in faith, it has a cumulative effect on the mind.

And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:7, NASB

This Scripture presents an image of peace as a guard over the heart and mind. This points to the reality that peace is not passive or fragile but protective. It is this protection that becomes more established, reliable, and accessible as a person cultivates faith and matures over a lifetime.

When Faith and Mental Health Work Together

Mental health care and faith are not competing forces. The most effective healing journeys often unfold when they work together. A person who is actively investing in spiritual growth is also cultivating a stable sense of identity that is not connected to performance or achievement. The result is an expansion of the capacity for hope even in difficult circumstances. These benefits are concrete qualities that support the goals of meaningful, lasting mental health care.

There are seasons when the weight of life requires more than spiritual practice alone. Grief, trauma, relational wounds, and clinical mental health conditions are real, and they deserve professional support. This is where Christian counselors bring a distinctive advantage.

A faith-based counselor understands the spiritual dimension of a person’s life, and they are equipped to help integrate faith into the healing process. This offers a meaningful, practical, and deeply personal strategy for those seeking genuine inner wellness and spiritual maturity.

Learn how your spiritual maturity and mental health connect

There are no shortcuts in developing spiritual maturity. It is a process with no finish line to declare the work complete. The growth that accumulates along the way, as trust deepens and views on hardship broaden, also produces genuine, measurable support for a healthy mind. Spiritual maturity is not a badge or a marker of having arrived somewhere. It is a way of life built one season at a time through the easy and hard years a person navigates.

Those who find themselves at the intersection of spiritual growth and mental health should know that the two need not exist in separate lanes. A maturing faith is a resource for lasting inner wellness, and pairing it with the right professional support makes a meaningful difference in how a deepening faith shapes mental health.

If you are ready to integrate your faith and mental health, please reach out to our reception team to be connected with a counselor who understands both and can help you begin this process. The reception team can provide you with more information about faith-informed counseling and how it can support this journey.

item.title: Severe Anxiety: Dealing with Medical Anxiety
item.description:
If you are one of the millions of people who suffer from medical anxiety, you know how crippling it can be. Logically, you may understand that seeking medical attention is the right thing to do to protect your health, but trying to get yourself to actually make and keep an appointment seems threatening and nearly impossible.

The difficult conundrum with medical anxiety is that it operates on an unfortunate and continual loop. When you fear the one thing that can stop the anxiety, it can make you feel not only trapped, but hopeless.

Can you get over medical anxiety? Yes, you can. Just like other fears and anxiety-based behaviors, through therapy and prayer, you can overcome these limitations and live a normal and healthy life. Read on to learn more.

What causes medical anxiety?

While you might be predisposed to anxiety through your biological makeup, most people aren’t born with this fear. It is something that develops after experiencing a medical trauma.

Maybe your beloved mother died of cancer, and now you fear every small anomaly you discover on your body. Or maybe you got an unfavorable diagnosis, and your anxiety has convinced you that every subsequent doctor visit will result in the same terrifying news.

There are a number of ways and reasons someone might develop medical anxiety. Whatever the cause, the resulting consequence is often insufficient healthcare, missed medical appointments, and delayed checkups. This can lead to an unhealthy lifestyle.

What characteristics make up medical anxiety?

Medical anxiety varies in type and severity. Some suffer from illness anxiety disorder (IAD), which is commonly known as medical anxiety or health anxiety. The definition, as given by the National Institutes of Health, is a psychiatric condition characterized by intense, persistent, and excessive fear of having or developing a serious, undiagnosed disease.

Some people have milder cases of medical anxiety and may simply refer to their condition as “white coat syndrome,” meaning they fear things related to doctors or medical facilities.

What does having medical anxiety actually look like? Here are some characteristics you might experience.

You catastrophize

If you have medical anxiety, you will likely assume the worst-case scenario is imminent for all things health-related. That little headache you have can become convincingly similar to a brain tumor. That skin tag, which is a normal part of aging, can look suspiciously close to a cancerous growth through the lens of anxiety. When you live in a constant state of threat, your brain scans for any new or additional information that could be a sign of a bigger threat.

You feel overwhelmed

Another unfortunate element of medical anxiety is the feeling of being overwhelmed. It’s not unusual for people to postpone routine checkups or visits for minor ailments. For those with medical anxiety, those missed appointments happen often and aren’t due to scheduling mishaps.

With every missed appointment, medical conditions can compound. A minor issue can develop into something more serious. When that happens, not only does the need to seek medical attention grow, but the fear of receiving devastating news grows right with it. Even if you want to get back on track with your health goals, seeing the number of appointments you would have to face can make the whole process feel like too much.

Your mind starts to reel as you recall the date of your last dental appointment. You notice your eyeglasses aren’t quite as effective as they used to be, and you don’t even remember the date of your last blood test. You know you should make those appointments, but trying to force yourself to do the thing you fear can feel nearly impossible, and the sheer number of these necessary appointments can feel overwhelming.

You’re preoccupied

When you suffer from medical anxiety, you have a persistent preoccupation or intense focus on having or contracting a serious illness. You may not have any real symptoms that would indicate imminent danger, but your anxiety reacts as if there is an actual risk.

You may try to comfort yourself by doing independent research on symptoms or early warning signs of danger. This information rarely brings peace and might easily trigger an even greater degree of anxiety.

You seek reassurance

Another common pattern in someone with medical anxiety is the constant need for reassurance. You might find yourself asking a spouse, family member, or friend if they think something is wrong with you. You go into painstaking detail about your symptoms, hoping they’ll tell you that you’re okay.

That works for a while. You feel relief, and your fears subside. But that peace is short-lived. Before long, the doubt will resurface, and you will wonder if they’re telling you the truth or if they are even confident in their own answer.

Your behavior changes

Your medical anxiety might not just affect your mind and emotions, but dictate your behavior too. You might excessively check for signs of illness, scanning your body for any anomalies or symptoms. Conversely, you might avoid medical offices and information altogether.

Getting Over Medical Anxiety

There may not be a magic switch that you can flip to suddenly feel fearless, but with slow retraining of your mind and body, you can learn to respond differently to your medical anxiety.

Therapy

One of the most effective ways to overcome this crippling fear is through therapy. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) can help you identify the thought patterns that fuel your anxiety and challenge them with truth. Instead of immediately jumping to worst-case scenarios, you can learn to pause and question those thoughts. You can also learn how to replace them with more realistic and reassuring ones. Eventually, this will weaken anxiety’s power over you.

Exposure therapy is another effective approach to overcoming medical anxiety. While exposure to the thing you fear the most might feel terrifying, you don’t have to force yourself into overwhelming and scary situations all at once. You can learn to take small, manageable steps instead.

Maybe you start by simply looking up a nearby doctor or scheduling an appointment. Even if you later cancel that appointment, you’ve made progress by exposing yourself to the idea of going to the doctor. Maybe you sit in the waiting room of a doctor’s office before you even make an appointment. Exposing yourself to the environment in a non-threatening way and knowing that your name won’t be called can help you build up a tolerance for medical environments.

Each step you take to expose yourself to medical situations can help build confidence. It trains your brain to feel safe, even when the threat feels imminent.

Trusting God

Much of the fear behind medical anxiety stems from a lack of control. You don’t know what’s going on inside your body, and that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But the good news is that God knows.

God created you wonderfully, and He knows every detail about you. While He never promised a life free of difficulty, He does promise His presence even in the face of adversity. When your brain starts to spiral into the “what ifs,” you can center yourself on what is the absolute truth. That God is with you and your life is ultimately in His Hands. Your lack of control doesn’t have to be a deficit, but can be viewed as faith.

Help For Medical Anxiety

If you need help getting past your medical anxiety, schedule an appointment with a Christian therapist. These professionals at this practice can help you overcome this crippling fear that not only affects your mind but can also impact your overall physical health. They can point you back to the all-knowing, all-powerful God who loves you and wants you not to live in this fear any longer.

item.title: The Trauma of Aging: Where to Find Support
item.description:
Is “trauma” too big a word for this situation? Aging isn’t a dramatic event with alarms, flashing lights, and a solitary life-changing moment. Yet, the evidence of aging in your own life and body can hit harder than you would ever expect. You knew you’d grow old, or at least you hoped you would. But you never knew what aging would actually feel like.

Saying that aging is trauma may not be clinically precise, yet it is emotionally true. Aging is not the trauma of tragedy or catastrophe. It’s natural, normal, and can be anticipated. But those small cumulative losses of independence, stamina, and your youthful good looks can chip away at the self-worth you’ve tried hard to build and maintain.

It feels like trauma

Aging, while natural, can be experienced like a traumatic event for some people. Aging, of course, does not happen in a single moment, but it can still make you feel as if you’ve experienced trauma. It deals with loss, grief, accumulated stress, and unrelenting reminders of your own mortality.

That ongoing exposure to loss and change can feel trauma-like, especially if it triggers anxiety, depression, panic, or reactivates previous trauma such as illness, neglect, abuse, or medical trauma. And it’s more prevalent in cultures that don’t value the aging process, as we see in the modern Western world.

Some therapists might label this as an existential trauma or cumulative trauma rather than a single event. But in strict clinical terms, aging itself is not classified as trauma in the same way that PTSD is defined. True trauma involves a singular or series of traumatic events that involve a threat to life or safety.

But, and this is a big but, your emotions can still feel similar to actual trauma from age-related events. True trauma is often associated with aging, such as medical procedures, loss of a spouse, chronic pain, or serious illness.

This means that aging, while not the singular trauma itself, is often the context in which true trauma can happen. And the process of aging can evoke emotions often associated with trauma because of your personal sense of loss.

I miss my strength and independence

Aging comes with a lot of changes, but these changes aren’t always obvious at first. The gradual loss of strength and stamina can truly alter how you interact with the world around you. What used to come easy, like a long walk or lifting heavy objects, suddenly requires more effort and even forethought. And for many, especially those who value their independence or are known for their physical strength, this is the most difficult age-related adjustment to accept.

But God doesn’t value you for what you can do, what you can lift, or how fast you can do it. In fact, having your own abilities stripped away can also strip away pride. When you can do all things by yourself, you no longer have to rely on God or others. “Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to Him, and He will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5-6, NIV).

Aging forces you to confront the truth about your body and its limited strength. “Leaning on God” does not just include your own “understanding” but your practical daily needs as well.

This mind shift can push you away from the feelings of loss toward surrendering your own pride. It can teach you gratitude as you learn to rely on family, friends, and community, and yes, to trust God to provide all these things for you. It also teaches patience, as you cannot always take care of your own needs in an instant. It might also teach you empathy for other people in your situation or push you toward asking for forgiveness for past impatient behavior.

I miss my village

With time comes seasons. And seasons change. As you age, not only do you have to deal with your own age-related issues, but you are affected by the changing seasons in others’ lives as well.

Spouses, family members, and lifelong friends pass away. People move after they retire. Adult children become increasingly independent, and you become acutely aware of the shifting dynamics.

You might suddenly feel out of place in a culture that is hyper-fixated on youth. You can no longer relate to the newest trends, and you don’t quite understand all the jokes that everyone else seems to find amusing.

But these circumstances, while they might feel lonely in the moment, are also reminders of the consistency and faithfulness of our never-changing God. The God you knew in your youth, He’s the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8, NIV). And even if you haven’t known God for long, you can be assured that He will never leave you or forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

I Miss My Good Looks

The world is obsessed with youth. Models in magazines have flawless skin and near-perfect physiques. The beauty industry is a multi-billion-dollar business built on the shallow fact that people crave beauty, from themselves and those around them.

So, when you look in the mirror and discover a new gray hair or a wrinkle that has gotten a bit deeper, the emotional impact you feel might feel can hit harder than you know it should.

You know that vanity isn’t a virtue you should be aspiring toward. You probably don’t even want to admit it because it seems so shallow. Yet it can shape how you see yourself and how worthy you feel of love, attention, and belonging.

And when you notice the physical changes in your appearance, it can not only undermine your self-esteem but can be a reminder of the loss of youth, and worse, the progression of aging.

But if you stop and ponder the Word of God, you will realize that maybe you shouldn’t have relied on your looks at all. Maybe this aging process actually weeds out a part of your being that shouldn’t have been there in the first place. That same God is using this process to refine you. Even those gray hairs are tools to draw you closer to the Almighty.

In that way, your focus shifts from what is being taken away from you to what is being revealed and rewarded. 1 Peter 3:3-4 says, “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles and the wearing of gold jewelry or fine clothes. Rather, it should be that of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit which is of great worth in God’s sight” (NIV).

Not only does your aging body help you focus more on what is truly important, your inner self, but it is in itself a reward. “Gray hair is a crown of splendor. It is attained by a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31, NIV).

Therapy

By the time you hit your golden years, you might think that you have everything figured out. You know how to manage your stress reasonably well. You’ve had trauma in your life and survived. But the scars you carry and that underlying, unresolved trauma can cause you to feel anxious, hypervigilant, or angry.

Even if you don’t feel the effects of past trauma, you will likely face new traumas as you age. Medical issues for you and your spouse, transitions such as retirement, moving into elderly care homes, or dealing with other age-related traumas exist.

Christian therapy can help you through these mental and emotional issues and transitions. It can help you understand your body, celebrate your life, and give you hope for a peaceful future. It can help you face your own mortality with acceptance and remove the fear and anxiety surrounding death.

If you’re struggling in the aging process, know that there’s help available to you. At Spokane Christian Counseling, we are here to assist you in overcoming your age-related fear, trauma, and anxiety. Contact our reception team today to help you live more peaceful tomorrows.

item.title: How to Stop Worrying: Is Certainty Your Idol?
item.description:
Most people have one fear or worry that looms larger than all others. Maybe you’ve been labeled the “worry wart” in the family because you tend to overthink or anticipate negative outcomes. Or maybe you don’t worry about everything, but you have that one thing that triggers you. You just don’t know how to stop worrying.

Whether you’re in a constant state of fear or you have that one unresolved trigger that has turned into more than a hyperfixation or phobia, you may be dealing with something deeper than anxiety alone. Beneath the surface, there may be a persistent need for clarity. You hold tight to the idea of living a secure, certain life. But could certainty be an idol?

What is an idol?

When we think of idols, we often conjure images of golden statues or ancient altars. Images of gold figures glisten in the desert sun, or chubby little gods may come to mind. But idols in the modern world, especially in the Christian faith, are rarely as obvious as a tangible item sitting on a home altar. An idol is anything you rely on to provide security or peace that isn’t God. An idol is anything that functions as a savior.

When certainty becomes a definitive goal, worry can become a ritual. You may not even realize you’re doing it, but when you crave certainty, you might start to believe that your worry is the catalyst to certainty. This is where certainty fails as a god. An idol might promise a reward, but it can’t deliver on it. You might chase certainty to find peace, but the chase only causes more chaos.

Is it a spiritual issue?

Overthinking about a problem or mentally preparing for a potential negative outcome can unconsciously convince you that, through this coping mechanism, you can somehow control the universe. As a result, you sacrifice your sleep, your relationships, or even your physical health at the altar of certainty. You hope that your mental suffering will act as an offering to the god of certainty.

Is a hyper-fixation automatically an idol? Hyper-fixation, even when it feels overwhelming and obsessive, isn’t automatically an idol. In many cases, a hyper-fixation can be the result of biological influence, trauma, and learned patterns of thinking. It’s a biological and psychological issue, not a spiritual one.

The nervous system often shapes anxiety, rumination, and intrusive thoughts. They are not simply created by personal choice. It’s important to acknowledge this in your own life and others’, because not every intense or persistent thought pattern is a spiritual issue.

The pattern of worry or need for certainty may have started as a way to cope or protect yourself in unpredictable situations. In a way, it may serve its purpose by making you feel more prepared for difficult situations. But without even knowing it, your need to prepare or your need for certainty can become a way you try to gain control rather than relying on God in moments of unpredictability.

You can’t automatically attribute the feelings of worry or anxiety to the sin of idolatry. If you do, you risk over-spiritualizing a biological reality and turning a biological and psychological survival response into a moral failure.

However, in some cases, these thought patterns can have a spiritual element. If you’re dealing with a need for certainty, it might be worth exploring whether or not there is a spiritual root.

Habakkuk teaches about worry

In Habakkuk 1, the prophet is witnessing the collapse of his society. His worry is rooted in real-world trauma, not necessarily a biological tendency. He’s dealing with violence, paralyzing laws, and justice that never prevails (v. 4). His anxiety is a rational response to an irrational world. Habakkuk’s trauma-informed response is exactly what a dysregulated nervous system looks like today.

Habakkuk does what many of us do in times of crisis or uncertainty. He asks, “Why?”

Seeking Certainty

Habakkuk’s “why” was a desperate cry and longing for clarity and a predictable end. He’s looking for a way to make the chaos all around him finally make sense. The book begins with a cry of anguish. “How long, Lord, must I call for help, but you do not listen?” (Habakkuk 1:2, NIV) This language may sound familiar because you have said it a few times yourself.

Maybe you feel that if you can find the right perspective or answer, the fear will stop. Yet God feels distant. This is a natural response. Asking “why” is not where the problem lies. In fact, it’s often the beginning of faith. The problem starts when the need for an answer becomes a condition of peace.

When that need for an absolute outcome outweighs your trust in God, certainty could be considered an idol. Unfortunately, certainty is often unattainable, as you want to take control of the uncontrollable. That might sound like a bit of a stretch, but when you break down the typical worry process, you see the striking similarities between the need for certainty and idol worship.

When you worry, you’re sacrificing your present peace for future certainty. You likely have rituals, much like the rituals in idol worship, that make you feel secure in the moment. You might rehearse the worst-case scenarios in your head, hoping not to be blindsided.

Scripture and psychology speak to certainty

Scripture and modern psychology hold similar insights when it comes to the human need for certainty. Both recognize that the mind is wired to seek predictability and control. This is particularly true in times of distress.

The difference is that Scripture frames this need as a matter of trust and ultimately, reliance on God. Psychology describes it in terms of cognitive patterns, nervous system responses, and coping strategies.

Where They Converge

The good news is that Scripture and psychology aren’t at odds with one another. When it comes to the need for certainty, they often work in tandem.

Therapists work with anxiety, obsessive thought patterns, and an intolerance of uncertainty. They examine how some people respond to the unknown with disproportionate distress. It isn’t the bad thing itself that is causing the most suffering, but the not knowing, the waiting, and the uncertainty.

Does this sound familiar? It’s the situation we see at the beginning of Habakkuk.

The goal in therapy isn’t to eliminate uncertainty because that’s impossible to do. But the goal is to help clients build a greater tolerance for that uncertainty. Through therapy, you can slowly train your mind and your nervous system to remain regulated even when the outcomes are unknown. This can be done through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and other methods that help your body feel safe even in moments of uncertainty.

Faith in God offers something remarkably similar. Scripture not only encourages you to tolerate the unknown but gives you an invitation to trust the One who holds your future. It gives you something to do with that anxiety while waiting.

God’s Perspective

It’s important to note that if you struggle with the need for certainty, God understands. He’s not standing on a distant planet, cross-armed, just waiting for you to have more faith. The same God who designed your nervous system understands why uncertainty feels threatening to it.

Psalms 103 says that He “knows how we are formed; He remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:14, NIV) That verse says that God understands your humanity.

Coming Back to Habakkuk

What makes Habakkuk’s story so powerful is that by chapter three, something has shifted. He hasn’t received all the answers he was looking for. The chaos around him hasn’t resolved, but his posture has changed.

He writes in chapter 3, “Through the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines… yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will be joyful in God my Savior.” (Habakkuk 3:17-18, NIV)

Habakkuk is making a deliberate, hard-won choice to anchor his peace in something that uncertainty cannot touch. He moves from “How long, Lord?” to “Yet, I will.” As small as that shift might look on paper, it is a remarkable transformation from the need for certainty. It is a shift from holding that need for certainty as an idol to relying on God as the solution.

You can change too

That same transformation is available to you. That process of transitioning from “How long, Lord?” to “Yet, I will,” might just start with a phone call. Call one of the therapists on this site today to get started.

item.title: Understanding Seasonal Depression in Men Through Faith and Awareness
item.description:
Changing seasons often bring more than just shorter days and colder weather. For some, it brings changes in mood or depression. It’s not just women who can be affected by seasonal depression; men can also fall victim to this mental struggle. The shift from summer to fall and winter can carry an emotional weight that is difficult to name. Men may brush this off as stress from work or the holiday rush, but underneath, it’s something more persistent.

Depression in men does not always look like sadness. It can sometimes wear the mask of irritability, exhaustion, or a quiet retreat from everything that once mattered. Seasonal Affective Disorder affects men differently than women, and the symptoms often hide beneath the layers of what society tells men they should be.

The challenge for men is to recognize when the seasonal changes become something more concerning. The messages men receive throughout their lives about strength and pushing through difficulty without complaint create a framework where acknowledging depression feels like admitting defeat. But recognizing the symptom is not a weakness; it is the first step toward healing and wholeness in Christ.

Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in Your sight, Lord, my rock and my Redeemer. – Psalm 19:14, ESV

Increased Irritability and Anger

xWhen depression in men presents during the winter months, it rarely announces itself as sadness. It often appears as a shorter fuse, such as frustration that erupts over minor inconveniences. He may find himself snapping at his children over homework or getting agitated in traffic. These are not character flaws, but rather symptoms of a brain chemistry shift. It happens when sunlight decreases and melatonin increases during the darker months.

The cultural narrative says that anger in men is more acceptable than vulnerability. When seasonal depression settles in, irritability becomes the primary language. Rather than admit feeling lost or overwhelmed, men think it is easier to be angry.

The result is a painful cycle where relationships suffer, guilt increases, and depression deepens. Some men may recognize that they are acting differently and struggle to connect these outbursts to seasonal changes affecting their mental health.

The reality is that anger itself isn’t sinful or bad, but it is what we do with it that matters. Emotional regulation can be sidetracked by seasonal depression, making it harder to process anger in a healthy manner. Christian counselors understand the intersection between brain chemistry, seasonal changes, and spiritual well-being. This allows them to help men distinguish between righteous anger and the irritability connected to depression. This can also allow space for men to heal without shame.

Be angry, and yet do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger. – Ephesians 4:26, NASB

Physical Fatigue and Loss of Energy

Seasonal depression is accompanied by exhaustion that feels different from normal tiredness. This type of exhaustion is a heaviness that makes getting out of bed feel like moving through concrete. It makes simple tasks become monumental efforts that seem to deplete every ounce of energy.

A man may need multiple alarms to wake up and struggle to focus during meetings. Some may be completely drained by mid-afternoon, and it’s not laziness. It is a psychological response to reduced sunlight that affects serotonin production.

Men often interpret this fatigue as a personal failure. They push themselves harder, drink more coffee, and berate themselves for not keeping up. The result leads to a series of contradictions that become unbearable:

  • Be productive yet acknowledge limitations.
  • Be strong but admit exhaustion.
  • Be present yet barely functioning.

These opposing demands create a vicious cycle where stress compounds the depression. The body is signaling that it needs rest and intervention, and cultural expectations are demanding that they push through.

Scripture invites us to understand that we are not designed to carry everything alone. Seasonal depression drains energy reserves in ways that human willpower alone cannot overcome. When men recognize physical fatigue as a legitimate symptom rather than failure, it opens the door to seeking help.

Through light therapy, vitamin D supplementation, adjusting sleep schedules, and professional support, men can get help with addressing the biological components of seasonal exhaustion.

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

Social Withdrawal and Isolation

One of the most subtle symptoms of seasonal depression is the gradual pulling away from relationships. Men may start declining invitations to gatherings and respond to text messages less frequently. His excuse may be that he is too busy or he needs space. The result is deeper isolation as he spends more time alone. What may start as missing one church service leads to missing several, and what starts as skipping one small social event leads to avoiding all of them.

Society dictates that men should be independent and be able to solve their own problems without burdening others. Men feed on this message and heed an internal whisper that no one wants to hear about struggles or that real men handle things privately. The withdrawal will continue, and eventually, he will become less connected and more isolated. He will not notice the relationships that can provide support and perspective due to the lies of depression leading to isolation.

We were not designed to handle all the stress of this world alone. God’s word encourages us to bear one another’s burdens and love one another as we love ourselves. Seasonal depression convinces men that solitude is preferable to openness, yet we genuinely need one another during difficult times.

Christian counselors can help men recognize the withdrawal patterns and help them rebuild connections. They can emphasize that seeking support is not a sign of weakness but rather a display of wisdom.

Two are better than one because they have a good return for their labor, for if either of them falls, the one will lift up his companion. But woe to the one who falls when there is not another to lift him up! – Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, NASB

Changes in Sleep Patterns and Appetite

The natural rhythms of the body are disrupted by seasonal depression. Men might find themselves sleeping more than usual or spending ten or more hours in bed and still wake up unrefreshed. Some may experience the opposite, lying awake for hours, unable to find rest, while the mind races with worries.

Sleep is not the only thing affected by seasonal depression. Changes in appetite can also be a symptom. Some may lose interest in food, and others may have intense cravings. The symptoms are as unique as each man.

Men often rationalize these changes so that they do not disrupt the idea of men handling things by themselves. They may blame work stress for poor sleep or justify the late-night snacking as a bad habit. When these patterns emerge specifically during the fall and winter and disappear during the spring and summer, they point to seasonal depression. The body responds to decreased sunlight by altering sleep, wake cycles, and appetite regulation.

With seasonal depression, disrupted sleep and appetite can affect every area of life. This means it’s vital to understand and address. They are symptoms that require attention and not choices or bad habits. Concentration suffers, moods can worsen, relationships become strained, and spiritual vitality decreases. It is essential to address these symptoms through proper sleep hygiene, nutritional support, and professional guidance.

Some men can benefit from light therapy boxes that simulate their exposure to sunlight, and others can adjust meal timing or supplement with vitamin D. These strategies can help regulate circadian rhythms, boost mood, and support overall energy levels. Consistency in daily routines and incorporating outdoor activities when possible can further enhance these effects.

Support Is Available

Men experiencing seasonal depression need to look beyond societal expectations and recognize their symptoms. These can include irritability, exhaustion, withdrawal, and disrupted daily rhythms, and are responses to environmental changes affecting brain chemistry and hormone production. It’s crucial to name these symptoms and seek the right professional assistance.

Christian counselors offer both clinical expertise and spiritual insight, understanding that seasonal depression is a legitimate medical condition that can coexist with faith. Treatment options may include therapy, light exposure, medication, lifestyle changes, or a combination. The important step is to reach out for help rather than enduring in silence. Connect with a counselor on this site or near you to learn more.

item.title: 5 Techniques that May Aid Self-Care for Anxiety
item.description:
The term “self-care” has taken a winding path in recent years due to its popularity in wellness communities. But self-care for anxiety is different. Evidence shows that it employs specific skill-based techniques to help reduce anxiety levels in those who suffer from generalized social anxiety.

More than a bubble bath or pedicure, self-care for anxiety is based on proven research supported by clinical trials. For example, mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) has been tested alongside medication-based treatment, and its findings in one study show that it offers comparable results to a specific, commonly prescribed medication for generalized anxiety disorder.

While one study doesn’t negate the use of medicine to treat anxiety, it does show that there’s hope in a layered treatment plan that includes a wide range of self-care for anxiety treatment.

Why MBSR Works in Self-Care for Anxiety

Much of the literature that has recently been released points to the efficacy of mindfulness intervention because it uses small, doable techniques that are simple to apply in the midst of everyday life. As opposed to a long-awaited rest-filled vacation or a specific self-care day of the week, MBSR gives a person practical ways to fuel calm throughout their week.

Another reason MBSR is often successful is that it can integrate multiple emotional regulation interventions that are interchangeable. Other benefits are that it has a high patient satisfaction rating, high levels of compliance, and, in some studies, even though MBSR can be used to treat other diagnoses, patients reported decreased anxiety levels.

Five Self-Care for Anxiety Techniques

One thing to keep in mind with each of these techniques is that self-care for anxiety is not a one-and-done treatment plan. In fact, incorporating each of these techniques into your everyday life is what fuels the reduction in anxiety levels. Trying a few breathing exercises once or twice, for example, will only help you in that particular moment.

However, if you’re incorporating breathing exercises multiple days each week, you may find that the exercises help you pay attention to your body and emotions throughout the day – one of the goals of mindfulness practices as a whole. Treating something you don’t see coming is much more difficult than treating something you can name, recognize, and have experience with.

You gain confidence that these techniques will work when you apply them in your everyday life, whether at work, at home, or at school.

Breathing: Many people recognize the benefits of deep breathing, but it has been proven to decrease anxiety in peer-reviewed studies by several reputable research companies.

Some options for breathing exercises include diaphragmatic breathing, paced slow breathing, breathing with biofeedback, and alternate-nostril breathing (ANB).

Low-Intensity Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: LICBT is a form of therapy that involves meeting with a practitioner on a short-term basis. You’ll receive tools to help you learn about stress management and anxiety-reducing practices.

LICBT is a type of therapy that allows for a cost-effective way to treat anxiety, particularly when someone has low to moderate generalized anxiety. It’s a series of tools that can be offered with practitioners and some without, particularly internet-based CBT.

For patients with cost barriers, online CBT can provide tools to help you learn more about the causes and treatments for anxiety. These can be delivered in the form of educational materials; apps that help you track your feelings, mood, and behaviors related to anxiety; and journals that help you assess situational anxiety.

However, any therapy available through an app will likely treat generalized anxiety. If you suffer from a different form of anxiety or you want more personalized attention, seeing a licensed therapist is preferable. This way, you can work one-on-one in a safe setting where you’re able to get regular feedback from a trained counselor about the anxiety you’re learning how to process.

Emotional Regulation Flexibility: Regulating emotions is a key component of anxiety reduction because it helps a person distinguish between their present reality and what they feel about their present reality – two different things.

ER flexibility has been shown to impact people suffering from anxiety because it teaches them how to integrate multiple tools – switching between them – to help lower their anxiety in various situations. Some of these tools include reframing your thoughts (discussed below) and acceptance.

Acceptance requires allowing your emotions, recognizing their triggers, and then deciding which strategy is best to employ. Instead of trying to avoid your emotions or distract yourself from them, this tool can be helpful when an outcome is out of your hands.

Sometimes called ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy), this tool recognizes why you’re feeling anxious, helps you admit that you are feeling anxious about something that’s outside your control (such as a test result), and then gives you enough pause to choose another strategy – such as disengaging from your anxiety because you know the mental spiral you’re in will not change anything.

Reframing: Also known as reappraisal, this practice involves challenging fearful beliefs related to situations that cause anxiety and transitioning fixed mindset processes to growth-oriented thinking.

Reframing can be incorporated into cognitive therapy, and it can help people who suffer from anxiety because it integrates new thought processes into everyday life. Applied regularly, reframing can help someone avoid rumination or looping thoughts that don’t lead to the abatement of their stress. In fact, spiraling thoughts can exacerbate cognitive stalling.

An example of reframing is when someone is in a social situation and they fear others’ unspoken responses. If you’re giving a speech, for instance, and you see a room filled with blank faces staring back at you, the anxious thought may be that they’re all bored, and you start to panic and lose your place. However, reframing would involve telling yourself, “They’re likely just concentrating on what I’m saying.”

Another example is when faced with an unknown, you start to feel your heart racing and your temperature rise. Physical cues could trigger anxious thoughts that convince you you’re not going to escape the situation. A reframed thought might be, “This is just how my body responds to stress, and while unknowns are challenging, they are to be expected in life. It’s okay to feel this, and these feelings will pass soon.”

Exposure Therapy: Exposure therapy involves addressing fears based on a scale, from lowest to highest, without safety mechanisms to run to.

In the presence of a licensed therapist, exposure therapy can gradually help someone address what causes their anxiety, slowly making the stimuli no longer elicit stress responses and therefore lowering their overall anxiety level.

A practitioner helps you rate what causes your anxiety from the greatest anxiety to the least, and you gradually address the anxiety-causing stimuli over time. By the end, you come to disassociate the fearful stimuli that once caused anxiety from stress. Instead, you associate it with a safe environment.

Self-care for anxiety can involve a variety of self-imposed tools and therapeutic tools, depending on your budget, how severe your anxiety is, and whether you’re comfortable meeting with a licensed therapist. If you’ve been fearful of meeting with a counselor about your anxiety, call one of our offices.

A caring staff member will walk you through what to expect at your first session, and you’ll be matched with a counselor who specializes in anxiety disorders.

Anxiety isn’t anything to feel ashamed of or be embarrassed by, as many people suffer from it in various forms. In fact, learning how to manage it through self-care for anxiety techniques is often helpful for anyone – teaching emotional regulation skills, how to think about what you’re thinking, asking if your thoughts are true, and learning to recognize anxiety triggers.

Many people gain such powerful life skills from learning about anxiety and how it has shaped them that they’re able to grow in their ability to manage setbacks, disappointments, and unexpected life circumstances throughout their lifetime. Learning how to manage anxiety is a skill that benefits your family, too.

Family members struggling with anxiety may struggle to interact with family members or attend family events related to their anxiety. Sometimes after a person has met with a counselor to address their anxiety, it’s helpful to attend family counseling so that their family members can help them with things like reframing and emotional regulation flexibility.

Of course, this depends on the family and how much siblings and parents have been impacted. But it can give them tools and language to help you and others impacted by this mental health condition.

To meet with a counselor and learn more about these self-care techniques, contact our office today and speak to a representative.

item.title: Coping with Grief During the Holidays Years After Loss
item.description:
It’s expected that the first few years after losing someone, the holidays are a struggle. People often understand that declining invitations and tearing up during Christmas dinner is all part of grieving during the holidays. But what about when it’s five or 10 years later? It seems the world assumes you’ve moved on, that the heartache has healed, and that you’re ready to face the holidays with nothing but a smile.

The reality is that coping with grief during the holidays doesn’t follow a timeline, and the assumption that it should can make holidays more isolating. Life has gone on without them, and you have created new traditions, gained new family members, and found moments of genuine happiness. Yet, when December arrives, the absence resurfaces in ways that catch you off guard and make you question whether you are making progress in your healing.

It’s not a confusion about grief. It’s about the expectation that you should have had enough time to erase it. Coping with grief years after the loss means that learning to heal and ongoing loss are not opposites. They appear together during seasons, centered on memory and tradition.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NASB

When Grief Returns After Years of Feeling Fine

There was a time when you thought you had it figured out, and the daily reminders had softened. You felt as though you had learned to live around the space that was left. Then the holidays arrive, and now you find yourself crying in the grocery store because you passed their favorite cookies. Maybe you become overwhelmed during a church service for reasons you can’t quite articulate.

This recurrence of grief doesn’t mean you have regressed or that your healing has unraveled. It simply reflects that there are seasons that carry concentrated memories. The holidays are dense with moments that remind you of who’s missing.

Long-term holiday grief can be particularly disorienting because it often arrives without warning. You have managed through other Decembers well, so you assume that this year will be the same. Then, out of the blue, you hear a song or a memory mentioned, and the loss feels fresh again.

Christian counselors understand that this pattern is typical. Grief is not linear, and anniversaries have a way of awakening dormant emotions. There’s no indication of weakness just because you are coping with grief years after the loss. It reflects the depth of connection that continues even when the physical presence is gone.

He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. – Psalm 147:3, NASB

Navigating Traditions with People Who Never Knew Them

There’s no doubt that your family has changed since you lost someone. You may have remarried, and children have been born. There are people who will never remember the person except through stories. New relatives have joined holiday gatherings, bringing traditions and expectations. It’s a natural and healthy evolution, even though it creates a complicated emotional landscape.

Trying to honor someone’s memory when most of the people at the table have never met them can seem uncomfortable. You want to respect the desire for a joyful holiday season, yet you’re not able to erase them from the celebration.

The challenge of coping with grief in a family is finding a way to acknowledge the loss without making it the center of everyone’s experience. This may mean quietly setting a place for them in your heart rather than at the table, or sharing a story or incorporating something they loved into the celebration.

Christian counselors can help identify authenticity rather than obligation or performance. The goal isn’t to maintain comfort at the expense of reality, but it’s also not to force grief onto people who didn’t share the relationship with the person who is no longer present at the holiday gathering.

This balance requires permission to honor your own needs while simultaneously recognizing that others are building their own holiday experience and may not place the same emotional weight on it.

A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance. – Ecclesiastes 3:4, NASB

The Loneliness of Long-Term Grief

In the early days, support was abundant as people were checking in and bringing meals to acknowledge your heartbreak of losing your loved one. But as years passed, the support typically faded, and the culture around you operated on the assumption that grief had a reasonable expiration date.

If you’re still struggling years later, or you feel as if something must be wrong with you, it can result in a particular kind of isolation during the holidays. You want to be grateful and cheerful, yet you quietly manage waves of sadness that others no longer recognize.

Sometimes you feel as though you must carry your grief secretly because there is a lack of social permission to express it in an ongoing way, so you find yourself smiling through holiday parties and internally navigating between celebration and sorrow. You try to participate in traditions, only to notice who isn’t there.

Everyone around you has moved on, so you may start to question your own feelings, thinking that you should be over it by now. That thought process reflects the cultural message we all hear about grief. The natural reality is that some relationships leave permanent marks, and the holidays have a way of making those marks visible again.

Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. – Romans 12:15, NASB

The Fear of Forgetting and the Guilt of Moving Forward

Long-term grief comes with a unique struggle of holding on and letting go. You want to remember everything about them, from their voice to their mannerisms. Memory, however, isn’t static, and as years pass, some details will inevitably fade.

The fading of memories creates a low-level panic during the holidays when you’re surrounded by reminders that also highlight what you can no longer recall with precision. You have built a life that includes joy and new experiences, allowing you to laugh at holiday gatherings while creating new traditions. Sometimes change and happiness bring a sense of guilt.

Coping with grief years after the loss has occurred involves navigating this tricky balance of honoring the past and not being trapped in it. Moving forward without feeling like you’re leaving your loved one behind often comes with intense anxiety.

Christian counselors understand that these aren’t competing goals and that remembering and living aren’t mutually exclusive. The love you had for your person doesn’t mean you have to remain frozen in that moment of loss, and experiencing new joy doesn’t diminish what they meant to you.

It is possible to experience a holiday that holds both memory and a connection to the present moment. You can miss someone and appreciate the people who are currently at your table. There are times the guilt that accompanies this duality is a signal that you’re holding yourself to an impossible standard. Moving forward doesn’t mean you’re forgetting, and remembering doesn’t require your constant sorrow.

For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. – Romans 8:38-39, NASB

Living with Grief That Has Softened but Not Disappeared

Grief often changes shape years after a loss. It is no longer the breathtaking pain of early bereavement, but instead it is quieter and more integrated into the fabric of your life. This does not mean it is gone during the holidays, and you may be surprised at how present it still feels. This is not a representation of failure, but rather a reality: some losses become a part of who you are, rather than something to get over.

Scripture promises comfort during these times, but it’s not always the absence of pain. It sometimes looks like the strength to carry both grief and gratitude in the same moment. This is a reflection of wisdom: knowing that you can honor a person and their memory as you fully participate in your current life. Coping with grief during the holidays years after is not about resolution, but about rhythm and learning the patterns of when grief tends to surface.

Holidays are likely to carry a significant degree of bittersweetness. Yet, they can become something you move through with honesty and hope, knowing that the love that causes the ache is the same love that makes the present meaningful.

Navigating the holidays can be difficult. If you’re struggling with grief years after loss, a Christian counselor can help. Call a counselor to learn more today.

item.title: Anxiety and the Sabbath Reset
item.description:
Work, family life, carpools, commutes, after-school activities, and errands, oh my! Life sure can get busy when you’re working or trying to raise a family. This feels even more so when you’re trying to do both. Living a fruitful life can be a blessing, but when it’s too busy, it can cause anxiety, stress, and even affect your physical health.

Don’t have time for a vacation? Can’t eliminate anything from your to-do list? While the occasional extended period of rest is ideal for recuperating from a busy lifestyle, it’s not always practical. But even the busiest people can spare one day a week to focus on rest. In fact, God wants you to. He called it Sabbath.

You Need Rest

You may think that pushing yourself even when tired and overwhelmed is an admirable thing. Of course, it is to a certain extent. It’s good to have the willpower and tenacity to stick with a project, even when you’re feeling overwhelmed by it. And this is often praised in our modern society because it’s labeled as a good work ethic. But there comes a point where that perseverance goes from noble to harmful.

Taking a Sabbath

God instructs us to take a Sabbath. Even He rested on the seventh day of creation. Is God giving you that direct command just to see if you’re obedient? This, like all of God’s other directives, is for your own good, not just to force you into compliance.

Of course, God values a good work ethic. This can be seen in multiple verses across Scripture (Proverbs 14:23, Proverbs 12:24, Colossians 3:23). But He also recognizes our need for rest. Jesus acknowledges this in Mark 2: “Then he said to them, ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.’” (Mark 2:27, NIV)

This verse explains not only God’s law but also gives a glimpse of His heart. God’s commandment to “‘Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy,’” (Exodus 20:8, NIV) is an invitation to you to step out of your normal, frantic routine and to take a day of rest to reflect on the goodness of God.

Psychologists Agree

Most psychologists and psychiatrists would give you the same advice that Scripture commands. That’s because those who study the human brain and emotions know that it’s not designed to live in a constant state of chaos and busyness. Your brain needs intentional periods of rest to maintain cognitive function and emotional regulation.

In the clinical world, this is often referred to as cognitive offloading. Without downtime, your stress response remains constantly activated. This can lead to anxiety. Maybe you’re familiar with this anxiety because you feel it every Monday morning. This happens because, without a Sabbath, you end up carrying the burdens of last week’s stress directly into the new week.

A day of rest works like a circuit breaker because it allows your nervous system to reset. While you might feel like you don’t have time to take a break, research shows that taking time to relax actually increases long-term productivity.

How to Take a Sabbath

Knowing that you should take a Sabbath every week is more than half the battle, but you also have to know how to do it well. Here are some ideas to help you make the most of your weekly respite.

Place God at the center

The original intent of the Sabbath was to carve out an intentional day, in the midst of a busy life, to honor God. And this idea still holds true today. To fully enjoy your Sabbath, you should, as the Bible directs, keep it holy. That means don’t crowd your day with mundane things. Instead, make an intentional plan to worship your Heavenly Father, to learn about Him, and to invite Him into your life every Sabbath.

When you place God at the center of your free time, you’re giving Him a special gift. You’re showing God you trust Him and honoring Him by giving your precious free time to Him. And when you do, He will reciprocate. Because the Sabbath is actually a gift to you from a Heavenly Father who knows how exhausting life can be.

Choose your day

Your Sabbath doesn’t necessarily have to be on Sunday, though that’s perhaps the most commonly observed day of rest. Most churches meet on Sunday, and many businesses close early, so it might be easier for you to not only avoid the distractions of errands but to find deliberate time with God.

For some, it’s not always practical to take Sundays off. You have to choose the day that works best for your schedule.

Establish rules

It’s wise to establish rules or construct boundaries for your day of rest because it’s important to protect this precious time. Rules and boundaries help you to keep yourself accountable and help others know what you are and are not willing to do on that day.

Maybe you are willing to hang out with friends and family, or perhaps you would be better served to spend the day alone. Maybe you want to sleep in late on your day off and don’t want to be disturbed, or you would rather get up early to watch the sunrise. By creating a few simple rules for yourself and others to follow, you can protect the peace of your special day.

Work smarter, not harder

One of the best ways to ensure that you can take a Sabbath day without filling it with stray errands is to find the most efficient ways to complete your errands during the week. That might seem like obvious advice, but it often goes unheeded. It’s good to occasionally pause and take a look at how you complete tasks. You might find that you do things out of habit, and you might not realize that there are newer, more efficient ways of doing these things.

For example, maybe you’re in the habit of paying your electricity bill by check every month. But have you explored the option of going digital with automatic payments? Many companies offer this service and even give a discount to customers who pay this way.

Don’t have the time to run to the grocery store? Use online shopping services or multitask by going grocery shopping with a friend. That way, you can get your socializing in while still completing a necessary task.

Working smarter gives you the opportunity to take a much-needed break, even if your life feels overwhelmingly busy.

Be prepared

When possible, prepare yourself and your surroundings for your day of rest. Make sure that the house is clean before your Sabbath day approaches and that your errands are taken care of. It’s difficult to fully relax in the midst of a chaotic reminder of future chores.

Have some of your favorite activities ready and at your disposal. Prepare a praise and worship playlist for some solo worship. Keep your Bible accessible, along with some highlighters and a notebook for a study of God’s Word.

You might also find that passive rest is beneficial. Gather a stack of books you’ve been meaning to read, some new video games, or create a list of bingeable television shows you can watch. Use these activities to truly decompress, not just kill time. Even more beneficial, get outside. Walk, relax, feel the sun. Resting in the beauty of God’s creation is a wonderful way to recharge on the Sabbath.

Seeking Professional Help

While the Sabbath is a powerful tool to help you strike a balance in your life, it’s also important to acknowledge that chronic anxiety sometimes requires more than just a day of rest. A licensed therapist or counselor can provide you with specific clinical tools that can help you overcome some of your deeper emotional challenges.

If your anxiety feels unmanageable, even in a season of rest, make an appointment with one of our Christian therapists. Our mental health professionals can help you take the courageous next step toward finding peace.

item.title: Anxiety Disorders: What They Are and What to Do
item.description:
What is anxiety?

We’ve all felt anxious about something. Adrenaline rushes in. Cortisol gives us that unmistakable sense of dread. Our heart races. Breathing becomes shallow. We tense up and sweat buckets, our head pounds, and our stomach aches.

While not a pleasant experience, anxiety can be a normal human response to stressors in our environment. Normal anxiety is a temporary and realistic response to pressures such as taking a test or interviewing for a job. Once the event is over, the anxiety resolves.

Anxiety is a God-given reaction meant to protect us from dangerous situations. When we feel unsafe, our body responds with one of four mechanisms: fight, flight, freeze, and fawn. Most of us are familiar with the first three. The fourth is a learned trauma response “where a person finds themselves responding to someone they perceive as dangerous by engaging in people-pleasing and submissive behaviors” (Fawning Trauma Response: Why It Happens & How to Stop, 2024).

These four responses in themselves do not signal that a person has an anxiety disorder. They are usually brief, resolve in minutes, and are triggered in proportionate response to our environment. So, when exactly does anxiety meet the criteria?

Diagnostic Manual Definition of Anxiety Disorders

Anxiety disorders, according to the DSM-5-TR, the American Psychiatric Association’s diagnostic manual, are “disorders that share features of excessive fear and anxiety… Anxiety disorders differ from developmentally normative fear or anxiety by being excessive or persisting beyond developmentally appropriate periods…typically lasting 6 months or more” (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

Consequently, the level and duration of fear and anxiety are key factors in what comprises a disorder. For example, two weeks spent stressing over an interview is normal. Suffering months of debilitating dread about the idea of being interviewed, and then sabotaging future employment opportunities because of it, is not.

Jesus tells us in Matt. 6:34 to avoid spending our life in chronic anxiety. He instructs us instead to deal with each day’s troubles as they come and not worry about troubles that haven’t yet taken place. He wasn’t just giving us a set of rules. Jesus knew that chronic worry leads to great harm if left unchecked.

Harmful Impacts of Chronic Anxiety

Healthline online breaks down the different impacts that long-term exposure to high stress has on the body. Physically, it can lead to excessive weight gain or loss. Cardiovascular issues could also arise, such as high blood pressure and heart disease, which increase the risk of coronary events such as heart attacks.

Other problems include digestive issues such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or chronic infections. Those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) “may be at an increased risk of hospitalization from anxiety-related complications” (Cherney, 2022). Muscle tension, depression, and isolation from social activities compound the issue.

Neurologically, the impacts of chronic stress are just as damaging. Stress triggers the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. This is the primary pathway that kicks in the fight, flight, freeze, and fawn reflexes. When the HPA is activated for too long, this can cause:

  • Hormonal imbalances that affect mood and cognition
  • Neurochemical disruptions that interfere with serotonin and dopamine (key players in emotional regulation)
  • Overstimulation of the amygdala, making you more anxious or reactive
  • Damage to the hippocampus, which is vital for memory and learning
  • Reduced function in the prefrontal cortex, impairing focus, planning, and decision-making (The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders, 2025).

When fight, flight, freeze, and fawn remain in overdrive, the autonomic nervous system never allows for the “parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) system that helps you recover” (Ibid). The brain needs this permission to rest and digest. Without it, lasting changes occur in the structure and function of the brain, which can lead to depression and/or anxiety disorders from an overstimulated amygdala (Ibid).

Types of Anxiety Disorders

Now that we have an idea of how anxiety affects the body and brain, let’s take a closer look at the actual disorders and their diagnostic criteria. Please note that this is a general overview of each disorder. It is not meant to be used for personal diagnosis. If you believe you or someone you know might have an anxiety disorder, please reach out to a licensed mental health professional for help.

The following are general overviews from the DSM-5-TR:

Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Diagnostic Criteria

Includes excessive anxiety about events or activities (such as work or school performance). Signs and symptoms are:

  • Restlessness
  • Getting tired easily
  • Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank
  • Irritability
  • Muscle tension
  • Poor sleep

Panic Disorder

Includes recurrent unexpected panic attacks. Symptoms of a panic attack include:

  • Palpitations, pounding heart, or accelerated heart rate
  • Sweating
  • Trembling or shaking
  • Sensations of shortness of breath or smothering
  • Feelings of choking
  • Chest pain or discomfort
  • Nausea or abdominal distress
  • Feeling dizzy, unsteady, light-headed, or faint
  • Chills or heat sensations
  • Paresthesia (numbness or tingling sensations)
  • Derealization (feelings of unreality) or depersonalization (being detached from oneself)
  • Fear of losing control or “going crazy”
  • Fear of dying

Agoraphobia

Includes excessive anxiety about two (or more) of the following five situations:

  • Using public transportation
  • Being in open spaces
  • Being in enclosed places
  • Standing in line or being in a crowd
  • Being outside of the home alone

Social Anxiety Disorder

Includes excessive anxiety about social situations. (Some examples: having a conversation, meeting a stranger, being observed eating or drinking, performing in front of others – e.g., giving a speech). The person fears negative evaluation, such as being humiliated or embarrassed, and being rejected by or offending others.

Specific Phobias

Includes excessive anxiety about a specific object or situation (e.g., flying, heights, animals, receiving an injection, seeing blood). The phobic object or situation provokes anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger posed by the specific object or situation.

Separation Anxiety in Adults

Includes developmentally inappropriate and excessive anxiety concerning separation from attachment figures. The individual may show:

  • Excessive distress about being separated from home or from major attachment figures.
  • Excessive worry about losing major attachment figures or about possible harm to them, such as illness, injury, disasters, or death.
  • Excessive worry about experiencing an untoward event (e.g., getting lost, being kidnapped, having an accident, becoming ill) that causes separation from a major attachment figure.
  • Reluctance or refusal to go out, away from home, to school, to work, or elsewhere because of fear of separation.
  • Excessive fear of or reluctance about being alone or without major attachment figures at home or in other settings.
  • Reluctance or refusal to sleep away from home or to go to sleep without being near a major attachment figure.
  • Repeated nightmares involving the theme of separation.
  • Repeated complaints of physical symptoms when separation from major attachment figures occurs or is anticipated.

The fear, anxiety, or avoidance is persistent, lasting at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents and typically 6 months or more in adults (Ibid).

OCD and PTSD

While OCD and PTSD are not classified as anxiety disorders, they do share overlapping mechanisms, including excessive fear or anxiety that significantly impact vocational and social functioning. It’s important to get help with these or any of the other disorders on the list, as they significantly affect daily functioning.

How Anxiety Manifests in Daily Life

Anxiety disorders negatively influence relational, educational, or vocational functioning. While acute stress might cause occasional disruption such as missing a day of work, chronic stress from an anxiety disorder has a much more outsized impact. Some of these impacts include:

Workplace – Procrastination, over-preparation, avoidance of meetings, burnout, loss of employment.

Relationships – Reassurance seeking, people-pleasing behaviors, conflict avoidance, explosive confrontations, emotional withdrawal.

Parenting – Hypervigilance, overprotection, difficulty tolerating child distress, or dissociation.

Decision-making – Rumination, fear of mistakes, avoidance behaviors, sticking with what is safe.

Treatments

These impacts can seem overwhelming. It may seem as if nothing can be done to resolve the never-ending cycle of dread that comes with having an anxiety disorder. But the following therapies from qualified mental health professionals are effective treatments:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): A licensed therapist trained in CBT helps clients identify, understand, and modify their anxiety-related thought and behavior patterns through regular sessions.

Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT): DBT incorporates the philosophical practice of dialectics, in which multiple or even contradictory ideas are examined, combining acceptance and change at the same time.

Exposure therapy: A form of therapy involving gradually exposing the individual to feared situations in a safe and controlled environment, with the ultimate aim of reducing the associated anxiety.

Group therapy: Refers to therapeutic settings that involve multiple participants in addition to a single healthcare provider (Anxiety.org, 2016).

Somatic Therapies: Somatically based therapies such as EMDR, IFS, or Lifespan Integration help individuals to integrate sources of trauma that may have triggered the initial disorder.

SSRIs, SNRIs, and Other Medications: While not therapies, antidepressants have been proven to be effective treatments.

Techniques for Managing Anxiety:

It’s good to note that we can also improve our anxiety prognosis through managing our own behaviors, emotions, and thoughts. This can be seen with techniques such as:

  • Mindfulness exercises and deep breathing exercises, prayer, or meditation.
  • Physical activities such as running, walking, yoga, cycling, etc.
  • Practicing good nutrition and limiting sugar, alcohol, and caffeine (The Connection Between Stress and Neurological Disorders, 2025).

Conclusion

Anxiety disorders are common and impact millions of people every day. With proper diagnosis, therapy, and techniques, anxiety can be treated. God desires our wholeness. As the Bible says:

…for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control. – 2 Timothy 1:7 ESV

Anxiety.org. (2016, December 9). Anxiety.org. Anxiety.Org. https://www.anxiety.org/treatments
