item.title: What Depression Feels Like and How It Affects Your Life
item.description:
Every year, approximately 21 million adults and 4 million adolescents in the United States experience at least one major depressive episode. There are likely more people who have struggled with their mental health in the last twelve months but who did not reach out for support or contribute to these statistics. Many of us do not truly know what depression feels like, how to deal with it, or when to get support.

All forms of depression are treatable with a combination of therapy, medication, and changes to your lifestyle. However, before you attempt to treat depression, you must first identify it. Once you have learned what depression feels like, you will be better equipped to handle it.

What Depression Feels Like

Your mind, body, and emotions are all connected and constantly affect each other, whether you realize it or not. For example, you will feel a physical illness in your body with symptoms like elevated temperature, difficulty breathing, or sore muscles, but the same sickness also affects your mood. Emotionally, you will feel more subdued, more in need of intimacy with others, and even a little hopeless. What is happening on the outside affects how you feel on the inside.

Sometimes the opposite is true; your emotions reflect in physical sensations and actions. When you are joyful, you might sing or whistle as you do certain tasks. When you are anxious, you might feel sweaty, and your muscles will tense in readiness for action. When you are disappointed, your shoulders tend to slump, your head feels heavier than normal, and you might struggle to make eye contact with others.

You can learn to identify what depression feels like, even though it is not a single emotion. You experience many different emotions during depression and feel various physical sensations. Depression affects your body, mindset, and mood. Over time, your habits, routine, and overall way of life can also be affected.

You might wonder why you are constantly tired, emotionally numb, and never in the mood to see your friends anymore. You could try treating these symptoms individually, but your diminished energy and motivation may significantly inhibit making a change.

People experience depression for multiple reasons. These could be things like grief, chemical imbalances in the brain, exhaustion from overwork, or mood disorders. To treat depression, we often begin by noticing the symptoms and then working back to the possible sources.

The best thing you can do for yourself is to be honest about what you’re experiencing and to speak with someone about it. If you have noticed any of the following changes in your life, consider reaching out to a loved one or professional for further support.

Increased Irritability and Anger

Anger, frustration, and irritability are often precursors or companions to depression. It is most noticeable in people who rarely lose their temper or show anger. If you are suddenly brooding and short-tempered, feeling impatient with everything and everyone, you might be battling depression.

Being in a constantly irritable mood will affect those who interact with you daily. Loved ones, acquaintances, and work colleagues will question you. At times you will deeply regret lashing out or losing your temper, but feel helpless to do anything other. You might benefit from anger management, or perhaps you have depression over an issue that needs addressing.

Changes to Your Appetite

Did you know that your eating habits often reflect your mental health? If there has been a recent change to your appetite with no medical explanation, this is often an indicator of what depression feels like. You might have an increased appetite, especially for sugary, salty, fatty food. These foods trigger dopamine production and can make you feel better emotionally, but only for a moment.

On the other hand, you might have a drastically decreased appetite, with no energy even for fast food. It’s not simply that you feel unmotivated to cook and clean up after yourself, but even eating feels like it would be a chore that you have no energy for. Unfortunately, this has a domino effect where your appetite leads to decreased energy, contributing to an even lower mood.

Constant Fatigue and Inactivity

Depression drains you of all enthusiasm and energy. One aspect of this is the dietary changes, causing you to have fewer nutrients and less energy. Another common aspect of depression-related fatigue is feeling overly anxious about the state of your physical health, but not having the motivation to do anything about it.

This sinks you lower into feelings of self-consciousness, self-loathing, and dramatically reduced self-esteem. As you begin to consider the tasks you have fallen behind in, you become so overwhelmed that, once again, you cannot find the energy or motivation to make the changes. It’s a cycle that can feel hard to escape.

Isolation

When you wonder what depression feels like, most commonly it feels like wanting to hide away from the world. So many of the habits we form when depressed are self-sabotaging. We need a better diet, some good sleep, some physical activity, and some friends around us, but we avoid these things and end up sinking even lower.

You avoid your friends and loved ones when you are depressed because you don’t want to burden them. Sometimes you can’t articulate or explain what you’re going through, and so it’s easier not even to try.

You might have friends who would confront or challenge you simply from seeing your appearance, and you’d rather not face it. Isolation feels protective, but it always makes things far worse. You need support, community, loved ones, and someone who will listen well.

Worsening Hygiene

At some point, you may have such a lack of motivation and energy that you stop caring for yourself practically. Your home becomes a mess of dirty laundry, empty takeout containers, and unpaid bills. Showering, brushing your teeth, and doing your hair feel like a chore that you cannot bother with any longer.

What depression feels like at its most extreme is an utter lack of energy and motivation to do anything besides the absolute basics of bodily functions. If you have reached this stage, you need help.

A New Path Forward

Dealing with depression is not for the weak or fainthearted. It takes guts, determination, and a strong spirit. Regardless of what mistakes or bad choices you have made until this point, the fact that you are still here reading this shows what resilience you have. However, you don’t have to struggle alone. You are not the first person to battle depression, and you won’t be the last.

Start to develop good habits now by reaching out. Learn to identify your emotions and the patterns of your mental health to help you get ahead of your mood swings. Remember that every season becomes new. Even in the dead of winter, there is new life beneath the surface waiting for spring.

If you have never considered counseling before, now is the time to reach out. When you are ready, we hope that you will find a suitable counselor who can provide the encouragement and hope that is in Christ to live well as an image bearer of God. You can call to speak with our reception team, who will be delighted to help you find the help you need.

item.title: What Are the Different Attachment Types and Why Do They Matter?
item.description:
Attachment Theory

In this modern age of pop psychology, many people are starting to hear about attachment theory. Some may even be able to tell you their exact attachment style. If you’re new to the idea of attachment theory, you may be curious about exactly what it is and what purpose it serves.

John Bowlby, a psychologist from the mid-twentieth century, founded the idea of Attachment Theory. In the 1950s, he described attachment behavior as behavior whereby an individual attains or maintains a connection to another clearly identified individual seen as better able to cope with the world (Bowlby, 1982).

Another psychologist, Mary Ainsworth, later tested his theory of connection with infants ranging from 9-30 months in age to see how they would react to short periods of separation from their caregivers (Ainsworth, 1978). Her findings, and the findings of later studies, informed the types of attachment styles and how these styles impact both children and adults.

Types of Attachment Style

“Attachment styles comprise cognitions relating to both the self (‘Am I worthy of love’) and others (‘Can I depend on others during times of stress’)” (Huang, 2026). Attachments begin in infancy. God designed us this way.

Consider the beginning of Scripture where God says, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him.” (Gen. 2:18, ESV BibleGateway.com). God’s original plan was to have a right relationship with Him and with others, just as He is in relationship with Himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Unfortunately, due to sin entering the world, our relationships with others are not perfect. Because of this, while secure attachments do exist, there are three types of attachment styles that are insecure: anxious-preoccupied, dismissive-avoidant, and disorganized, otherwise known as fearful-avoidant. The following excerpt from Simply Psychology has a breakdown of each:

Secure Attachment: Securely attached individuals are comfortable with intimacy and can balance dependence and independence in relationships.

Preoccupied Attachment (Anxious in Children): Individuals with this attachment style crave intimacy and can be overly dependent and demanding in relationships.

Dismissive Attachment (Avoidant in Children): This style is characterized by a strong sense of self-sufficiency, often to the point of appearing detached. Individuals with dismissive attachment value their independence highly and may seem uninterested in close relationships.

Fearful Attachment (Disorganized in Children): Individuals with a fearful attachment style desire close relationships and fear vulnerability. They may behave unpredictably in relationships due to their internal conflict between a desire for intimacy and fear of it (Huang, 2026).

A further breakdown of the behaviors that help identify each attachment style is as follows:

Secure

  • Healthy communication and management of conflict
  • Healthy view of self, others, and God
  • Regulated emotions
  • Ability to trust and connect with self, others, and God
  • Feeling comfortable alone
  • Being emotionally available for others

Anxious-Preoccupied

  • Feeling unworthy of connection
  • Highly sensitive to criticism
  • Uncomfortable with being alone
  • Low self-esteem
  • Difficulty with trusting self, others, or God
  • Feelings of jealousy
  • Fearing rejection or abandonment

Dismissive-Avoidant

  • Strong sense of independence
  • Easily dismiss others
  • Difficulty with trusting others or God
  • Avoiding emotional or physical intimacy
  • Having issues with commitment

Fearful-Avoidant

  • Having difficulty trusting self, others, and God
  • Struggling to regulate emotions
  • Showing signs of both anxious and avoidant attachment styles
  • Fearing rejection
  • Showing signs of confusing and contradictory behaviors (Cleveland Clinic, 2026).

Examples of Each Attachment in the Bible

Forming attachments is an unavoidable part of the human experience. Whether we have a secure or insecure attachment, the type we possess has wide-ranging consequences for how we view ourselves, others, and even how we view God. The following biblical figures map these styles with startling accuracy:

Secure

Ruth, who followed Naomi after the death of her husband and entrusted herself to Naomi and to God.

“Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” – Ruth 1:16, ESV

John, the beloved disciple of Jesus, to whom Jesus entrusted his mother.

When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold your son!’ Then he said to the disciple, ‘Behold your mother!’ And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. – John 19:26-27, ESV

Anxious-Preoccupied

King David, who openly expresses throughout the Psalms his fear and anxiety of being abandoned by God.

“O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath! For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me…O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you. My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes – it also has gone from me…Do not forsake me, O Lord! O my God, be not far from me! Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!” – Psalm 38:1-2, 9-10, 21-22, ESV

Dismissive-Avoidant

Jonah, who, at God’s call to witness to the Ninevites, fled the complete opposite direction.

Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.’ But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord. – Jonah 1:1-3, ESV

Fearful-Avoidant

The nation of Israel after God saved them from the Egyptians, led them with pillars of cloud and fire, gave them water in the desert, and fed them manna from heaven.

Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, ‘You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die.’ – Exodus 20:18-19, ESV

While these are exemplary models of specific attachments, I do not mean to suggest that these people can be universally typed according to Attachment Theory. Rather, these examples model known attachment behaviors and are thus useful for informing this article.

What is Earned Secure Attachment?

If you have read through and identified with any of the insecure attachment behaviors, the good news is that your attachment is not set in stone. Whether you had a difficult childhood that has led to trust issues, fear, and anxiety, or whether adult relationships have damaged your sense of self and trust in God and others, healing is possible.

Through therapy, forming healthy relationships, prayer, and practicing gentle self-reflection, you can build an earned secure attachment style.

But what exactly does “earned secure” mean, and what does it look like? A person with an earned secure attachment has “achieved a secure relationship with their own story. They can discuss their past clearly, acknowledge its impact on them, and hold their early caregivers with a mixture of realism and compassion – without being overwhelmed by grief, dismissive of the experience, or incoherent when describing it. (Simply Psychology, 2026).

EMDR, Lifespan Integration, Internal Family Systems (IFS), or other attachment-based therapies have proven effective in healing attachment wounds and moving clients toward forming stronger, healthier relationships with self, God, and others.

If you’ve found this article helpful in identifying an insecure attachment in yourself, it is never too late to take the first steps toward transforming how you view yourself, others, and even how you view God. God wants you to live life to the full. Therapy can help you get started.

References:

Bowlby, J. (1982). Attachment and loss: Retrospect and prospect. American Journal of Orthopsychiatry, 52(4), 664–678. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-0025.1982.tb01456.x
Huang, S. (2026, April 20). Attachment styles in relationships. Simply Psychology. https://www.simplypsychology.org/attachment-styles.html
Professional, C. C. M. (2026, February 13). Attachment styles. Cleveland Clinic. https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/25170-attachment-styles
Simply Psychology. (2026, May 15). Earned Secure attachment: How adults can develop a secure attachment style. https://www.simplypsychology.com/articles/earned-secure- attachment

item.title: Forgiveness: Bible Verses to Help You Forgive
item.description:
Forgiveness is a topic that sounds easy enough in principle but often feels impossible to put into practice. I remember the grief I felt years ago when the missionary organization I was serving painted me as sexually immoral, sent an email to every religious authority in the small country I was serving in to beware of me, and then let me go with zero proof of actual “sin,” and zero chance for me to defend myself.

This baseless spiritual abuse nearly drove me away from God. It took years before I could forgive my accusers.

We all know the pain of unforgiveness. The one that keeps us awake at night. The one that twists inside us like a knife. How can we extend forgiveness when the person we’re angry with has done the unthinkable? Doesn’t God know what they did to us? How then can He demand we forgive them?

Neuroscience of Resentment

Before we dive into Scripture, I’d like to point out that there are scientific reasons to back up God’s wisdom when it comes to forgiveness. We all know that refusing to forgive an offense can spiral into resentment and bitterness.

As shown in neuro scans studying the effects of unforgiveness, “[r]esentment creates a self-perpetuating cycle (Clark, 2005, as cited in Cherry, n.d.). When you replay what happened, you reactivate the same neural pathways, strengthening the emotional intensity of the memory through long-term potentiation (Kumar, 2011, as cited in Cherry, n.d.).”

This means that the more you ruminate on an event, the more it gets reinforced in your brain’s neural networks, leaving you stuck in the past and secreting cortisol, the stress hormone. Over time, the constant secretion of cortisol and the hyperarousal of the amygdala due to unresolved stress lead to depression, anxiety, and lower self-worth.

“Unforgiveness also correlates with sleep disturbances, cardiovascular problems, elevated blood pressure, weakened immune function, and increased inflammation markers (Abohashem et al., 2024 as cited in Cherry, n.d.; Segerstrom & Miller, 2004 as cited in Cherry, n.d.).”

Rumination leads to cortisol buildup over time. This is due to chronic stress. “Chronic stress causes the muscles in the body to be in a more or less constant state of guardedness. When muscles are taut and tense for long periods of time, this may trigger other reactions of the body and even promote stress-related disorders” (American Psychological Association, 2024).

These stress-related disorders include migraines or chronic headaches because of muscle tension in the neck, shoulders, and head. There are several more systems in the body that get triggered, including the endocrine system, HPA axis, gastrointestinal system, among others (Ibid). Needless to say, unforgiveness is a life stressor that can have far greater consequences than one might expect.

God, creator of the human body, knew this well before the advances of Western medicine. This is why He is so clear in Scripture that forgiveness is essential, not only physically, but spiritually as well. But what exactly does God mean by forgiveness?

What Biblical Forgiveness Is

The purpose of this article is not to use Scripture as a shaming device for those struggling to forgive. There’s a wide misconception about what biblical forgiveness means and what our Western culture makes it out to be. We often think God is asking us to forgive and forget, restore the full trust we had before the offense, or even excuse bad behavior. This is not what the Bible teaches.

If your brother sins against you, go and tell his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you, that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. – Matt. 18:15-17, ESV

Let’s take a closer look at what Jesus is saying in this passage. By using the word “brother,” He’s speaking of a person in the church, i.e., a Christian. Jesus advocates for private reconciliation between Christians wherever possible. He also makes it clear that He’s not speaking of trivial charges, but those of serious merit that can be corroborated by two or three witnesses.

The Greek word used in Matt. 18:15 is a variant of the word hamartánō, which is an archer’s term for missing the mark. A deeper dive into the word explains, “properly, having no share in; to sin, which always brings forfeiture – i.e., eternal loss due to missing God’s mark” (Strong’s Greek: 264).

If this Christian “brother” has refused to reconcile privately despite ample evidence of their wrongdoing, only then should it be brought before a spiritual body. If the offender does not listen to the church and witnesses, they are considered an unbeliever, and thus an outsider to the congregation.

The individual initially seeking reconciliation is also instructed to see them the same way. This denotes removing the closeness and the trust the offender held formerly.

Let’s be clear. Jesus isn’t saying, “Don’t forgive.” By making the offender an outsider of the church, Jesus is providing a way for shame to lead the offender to repentance. Once again, Jesus’ goal is for repentance and forgiveness between Christians, not for Christians to hold grudges or remove fellow believers from the church. Removal from the church is a means to bring the offender to repentance.

Forgiveness is further demonstrated in Matt. 18:21-22, where it says, “Then Peter came up and said to him, ‘Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?’ Jesus said to him, ‘I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven’ (ESV). Jesus asks that we forgive indefinitely. But once again, if the brother doesn’t repent, He’s not asking us to be pushovers.

If we focused solely on these passages, we might think God only asks us to forgive other Christians. But that’s not what’s implied in Matt. 5:44 when Jesus says, “But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (ESV). Paul gives a full description of what it means to love in 1 Corinthians 13.

In 1 Cor. 13:5, love is described as keeping no account of wrongs. The word used is the Greek logizetai. “The term appears in moral contexts where believers weigh motives and actions: 1 Corinthians 13:5: love keeps no account of wrongs;” it does not keep a mental ledger for retaliation (Strong’s Greek: 3049).

So, to love enemies is to keep no account, i.e., no ledger of the wrongs they’ve done against us. The antidote to our vindictiveness toward enemies is given in the same verse in Matt. 5:44, when Jesus tells us to pray for them. By praying for them, we are leaving God room to work on the hearts of our persecutors and replacing bitterness in ourselves with loving, restorative action.

Jesus doesn’t stop with asking us to forgive our brothers (Christians) or enemies (persecutors). He also asks us to love our “neighbor,” which again implies keeping no record of their wrongs. This is evident in Mark 12:31 when Jesus says, “The second [commandment] is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these” (ESV).

Neighbors, as we know from urban living, can be anyone – a Christian, an enemy, a non-Christian, even a complete stranger. Jesus’ command for forgiveness is thus universal. We are to forgive everyone regardless of their believing status.

Two further verses that back this up are Ephesians 4:32: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ibid), and Colossians 3:13: “[Bear] with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, [forgive] each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (ESV).

The Commandment to Forgive

Forgiveness is a command. Notice again in Colossians 3:13 where it states, “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.” (ESV, emphasis added)

We don’t get a free pass here. Even if we’re angry, even if the offense was great, even if we’re still hurting, we must forgive. Jesus doubles down on this in Matt. 6:14-15 when he says, “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (ESV).”

Paul tells us in Romans 12:18-21: If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good (ESV).

Conclusion

God doesn’t want us to ruminate. He doesn’t want the chronic stress of unforgiveness to destroy us. He calls us to action. Love our enemies. Pray for them. Do good to them. Feed them. Quench their thirst. Leave God to choose how He wishes to respond to their wrongdoing. There’s so much wisdom in these commands. Psychologically, action is infinitely more healing than inaction.

Forgiveness is a process. We aren’t expected to instantly be okay with what happened to us. With God’s help and our obedience, forgiveness is possible. Even when it feels anything but.
